topic: Should a four-person neighbourhood bakery open on Sundays when two of its staff already work six days a week? Make assumptions explicit and identify the information needed before deciding.
researchSummaries: Coverage is partial. Four jurisdictions were searched once each, and several requested items were not found. UK: Workers get a 24-hour rest in each 7 days, or 48 hours in each 14 [c_affe4efa]. The page describes limits only for large shops (280 sq m or more), so small shops appear to face no Sunday opening limit, though the page does not say so outright [c_affe4efa]. Shop workers can opt out of Sunday work without giving a reason, and are protected against dismissal and unfair treatment for doing so [c_affe4efa]. The notice period is three months if the employer gave the option within two months of starting. It is one month if the option was not given, and the 2016 changes reduced it to one month for large-shop staff [c_affe4efa]. No statutory Sunday premium was found. California: Labor Code 551 and 552 give one day's rest in seven, assessed per workweek and not on a rolling basis [c_a81346ae]. Premium pay applies only to employees who must work every day of the established workweek [c_a81346ae]. Section 556 exempts employers when hours do not exceed 30 per week or six in any one day [c_a81346ae]. No general Sunday premium was found. Australia: One secondary source (not read in this check) gives the General Retail Award Sunday rate as 200% [c_4610f6bf].

No source splits a new Sunday into incremental revenue versus revenue shifted from Saturday for an independent bakery, and that gap is the main finding. Three partial pieces follow. 1. Weekend concentration. A vendor KPI page says Saturday and Sunday typically carry 42-55% of weekly revenue at independent retail bakeries, with a Toast 2026 median of 48% [c_ea1cc387]. Individual bakeries vary: Tatte runs near 40% and Dominique Ansel above 55% [c_ea1cc387]. This is a benchmark range, not an audited dataset, and it does not separate Sunday from Saturday or say whether those bakeries open on Sundays. 2. Weekday profile. Statista has a revenue index of Dutch bakeries by weekday, based on January 2019 data [c_946217bd]. The extract shows no index values, so no Sunday or Saturday figure can be quoted. 3. Cannibalization analogue. A specialty retailer, not a bakery, opened stores two hours earlier on Saturdays and compared test stores with matched controls [c_63c5f899]. Saturday gross profit rose 8.4% ($210) and Sunday fell 1.1% ($28), against $170 of added cost. The source reports a net loss of $43 per store on average, although those three figures do not sum to that result [c_63c5f899]. Targeting only the stores where the change was profitable gave $2.5M of incremental annual profit [c_63c5f899].

Wages: the UK National Living Wage for age 21 and over rose from £12.21 to £12.71 an hour in April 2026, a 4.1% rise [c_e18b5042]. It applies to full-time, part-time, zero-hours and casual contracts [c_e18b5042]. It is the legal floor for adult counter staff. Under-21 minimums are £10.85 for ages 18 to 20 and £8.00 for ages 16 to 17 [c_e18b5042]. An aggregator puts the UK bakery assistant average at £12.32 an hour (July 2026) and bakers at about £14.10 [c_3ee9c7ca]. I could not check that page, so treat both figures as weak benchmarks. The assistant figure is below the adult NLW, so it probably includes under-21 rates. Budget at or just above £12.71 for adults. No source found sets a statutory Sunday premium. Time to hire: a general UK figure says average time to hire reached eight weeks, up from just under five a year earlier [c_b68f650d]. I could not check this page. It is not specific to bakery or part-time roles, and its date was not confirmed. Turnover: hospitality is the highest-turnover UK sector. The CIPD population-level measure puts it at about 52%, against a UK average of about 15% [c_b1638d1c]. RotaCloud's 2024 employer data shows 38.7% for hospitality and catering [c_b1638d1c]. Another report puts monthly leavers at about 6% [c_1125d5a4]. None of these is bakery-specific.

Sunday rates for bakery staff depend on which award covers the shop. All figures come from secondary pay-rate sites, and the primary award texts were not read.

Fast Food Industry Award (MA000003): one site gives 150% of base for Sundays, with casuals also at 150% [c_4610f6bf]. The Saturday 125% figure and the 2017 penalty review cut to Level 1 Sunday rates rest on sources I could not read [c_279d1285][c_8e051f32]. Check the award text [c_e4408167].

General Retail Industry Award (MA000004): two sources give permanent staff 150% on Sundays, $41.71 an hour at Level 1 [c_98834dee][c_1c060e54]. Source 1 conflicts, giving 200% for retail permanents and casuals [c_4610f6bf]. Casual retail treatment is unsettled: one source says 175% including the 25% loading [c_1c060e54], another says 200% of base [c_4610f6bf]. The earlier claim that source 5 describes casuals as 1.5x the loaded rate is not in its extract.

Source 6 says counter staff in a franchise bakery sit under the Retail Award, while production bakers may fall under a food manufacturing award [c_1c060e54]. Coverage is unconfirmed.

The 4.75% minimum-rate rise is not stated in the extracts. Source 1 shows the national minimum wage moving from $24.95 to $26.44 in July 2026. Confirm the shop's award, classification and the Fair Work pay guide before costing Sundays.

A UK employer can rely on a signed opt-out from the 48-hour average weekly limit if it is voluntary, in writing, and the worker is 18 or over [c_c70d0dea][c_b1ab34c7]. Workers cannot be sacked or treated unfairly for refusing, and it cannot be a collective agreement with the whole workforce [c_c70d0dea][c_b1ab34c7]. A worker can cancel at any time on at least 7 days' notice, up to 3 months depending on the agreement [c_c70d0dea][c_b1ab34c7]. The 48-hour limit is averaged over 17 weeks [c_b1ab34c7], so six shifts a week may not breach it anyway; that depends on shift length, which the sources do not settle. The opt-out does not cover night work. A night worker (usually at least 3 hours in the night period, by default 11pm to 6am) is limited to an average of 8 hours per 24 hours and cannot opt out [c_b7408307][c_b1ab34c7]. Whether pre-dawn bakers qualify depends on their start times. Records: the employer must keep a record that workers have opted out [c_c70d0dea]. Sources 3 and 5 were not read, so the detail on lists and signed copies is unconfirmed. For night workers, keep hours records showing the 8-hour limit is respected, for 2 years from the date made [c_b7408307]. Employers must offer a health assessment before someone becomes a night worker, with repeat assessments as reasonable [c_b7408307].

The extracts do not give a Sunday versus weekday unsold-stock waste rate for UK independent bakeries. Both cited pages report on the same Too Good To Go survey of bakery employees (255 employees and 2,024 consumers polled) [c_c189ea1a][c_9e6a9670]. They cover attitudes and causes of waste: 35% cite strict health and safety guidelines as the top reason [c_c189ea1a][c_9e6a9670], and 31% say weather affects demand [c_c189ea1a]. Ready-made sandwiches are the most wasted item, named by 58% of employees, followed by cakes (42%), fresh bread (37%) and pastries (36%) [c_9e6a9670]. Neither page splits waste by day of the week. The draft said it saw only search-result summaries; the extracts now show full article text, and neither contains the roughly one-fifth unsold or 16% production waste figures mentioned in the draft, so those stay excluded. The panel should not assume a typical Sunday waste rate from published data. The founder's own till and waste records are the best basis, and the bakery's Saturday unsold rate is a possible proxy, though that is a judgement and not something the sources state. Any Sunday waste figure in the debate should be labelled as an assumption.

decision.motionTitle: Sunday opening, and on what terms
decision.decision: Do not open on Sundays now. Sunday stays shut until four gates pass in order. Gate one: the two six-day bakers' last eight weeks of timesheets and signed contracts are checked against the 24-hour weekly rest rule and the non-waivable 8-hour night-work average, and any breach is fixed first. Gate two: counter staff, inside paid hours and never the two bakers, record six Saturdays of sell-out times per core line plus a tally of customers who ask for a sold-out item. Gate three: a written combined Saturday-plus-Sunday break-even is produced that nets out switched Saturday trade, holds existing Saturday wages and contracted hours fixed, costs Sunday waste separately, and includes the £640 weekly crew, about £550 notice exit and a provision for losing a baker. Gate four applies only if the tally clears roughly twice (£1,070 divided by the founder's actual average basket) asks per Saturday. In that case, run a time-limited trial on three fixed-term Sunday-only contracts with the end date and kill test written in, plus a separately signed variation for about six midweek par-bake hours from a shorter-week staffer. Neither six-day baker works a Sunday hour or a par-bake hour.
decision.rationale: The only lawful staffing the room found was three Sunday-only hires plus par-bake hours, about £640 a week, and that needs about £1,070 of genuinely new weekly takings at a 60 percent margin. Marisol's own estimate of the Sunday ceiling, about £650 with half of it switched from Saturday, leaves about £325 new and £195 contribution, and even zero switching gives only about £390. Once Priya showed that switching nets to nothing across the weekend, the case for opening rests entirely on unmet Saturday demand the founder has never counted. This ruling accepts the risk of a wrong no, which is forgoing Sunday profit for about two months, to avoid a wrong yes: three hires that are hard to unwind and a repeat of Marisol's head baker walking out.
dependsOn: The bakery is in the UK. If it is in Australia or Germany, penalty rates or Sunday bakery limits require the legal and cost analysis to be redone.
The contribution margin net of waste is about 60 percent.
The Sunday crew costs about £640 a week at roughly £15 loaded per hour, with no contractual Sunday premium.
A reduced Sunday range takes no more than about £650 to £700 a week.
Half of Saturday askers would return on a Sunday. Priya rated this low confidence, and it sets the ask threshold.
A tally of customers who ask for a sold-out item is a usable floor for unmet Saturday demand.
One of the shorter-week staff will voluntarily sign a variation for the midweek par-bake hours.

dissents.position: The bigger risk is not Sunday but the existing six-day pre-dawn pattern. The founder may need to restructure it even if Sunday never opens.
dissents.reasoning: If either baker is a night worker averaging over eight hours, no opt-out cures it. One tribunal award or one resignation would cost more than a year of the Sunday contribution argued over. Any written trial rota would also become evidence against the founder.

tripwire.signal: The eight weeks of timesheets show either baker averaging more than 8 hours per night shift, or a week without 24 hours of uninterrupted rest (or 48 hours per fortnight), or more than a 48-hour weekly average with no signed opt-out.
tripwire.by: When the eight weeks of timesheets are reviewed, before the first counted Saturday

dissents.costOfIgnoring: A live working-time claim or the loss of a long-serving baker, which Conor puts above a year of Sunday contribution. The founder also loses any lawful basis for a later Sunday trial.

dissents.position: The break-even is not honest until it carries a costed line for losing a baker. That line is still unpriced.
dissents.reasoning: Her failed Sunday cost her a head baker after eight weeks. She believes losing a key baker costs more than a Sunday trial earns. With roughly eight weeks to hire and four training Saturdays, that cost could dwarf the £445 weekly gap.

tripwire.signal: The written combined break-even reaches the founder with no figure for replacement hiring, cover wages and training Saturdays, or either six-day baker raises fatigue, asks for fewer hours, or resigns.
tripwire.by: When the written break-even is produced, before any Sunday hire is signed

dissents.costOfIgnoring: A trial that looks viable on paper fails on the first resignation. Eight weeks of lost production capacity and a repeat of the Bristol failure follow.

undecidable.question: Can this founder's bakery generate the roughly £1,070 a week of genuinely new weekend takings a lawful Sunday crew needs? The no rests on Marisol's untested £650 ceiling and Priya's assumed one-in-two return rate. Both were imported from other shops, not computed from his.

Second, the founder's actual average basket and Saturday takings from his till, to compute the threshold as twice £1,070 divided by his basket. Third, his unsold-stock sheets to set the waste-adjusted margin, replacing the assumed 60 percent.

That's eight hours before anyone counts the dough they mixed at the end of yesterday's shift. Do that six days running and the 24-hour rest might just squeak through, but the night-work average is the one I'd bet is already being broken, and nobody can sign that away. decision.motionTitle: Fix the six-day pattern before any Sunday trial
decision.decision: Before any Sunday trial, and whether or not Sunday ever opens, the founder pulls the last eight weeks of timesheets and the signed contracts for both six-day bakers. He checks them against 24 hours' weekly rest, the 48-hour average over the reference period (and whether either baker has signed an opt-out), whether either baker is a night worker under the contract's definition of night time or the default 11pm to 6am, and if so the 8-hour night-work average. Any breach is fixed in the current rota within the same pay cycle it is found, before any Sunday hour is planned.
decision.rationale: This ruling rests on cost asymmetry and settled law, not on a finished argument. The argument was cut off after one round: Conor and Priya never spoke, and the strongest objection (that a 4am start may fall outside the night-worker test, which would make the non-waivable limit irrelevant) was never raised or answered in the room. A wrong yes costs a few hours of checking records, while a wrong no leaves a possible existing breach running that cannot be undone, so this ruling accepts the cost of a wrong yes. Everything about the founder's actual bakers is assumed, because Marisol's 4am-to-noon pattern was seen in other shops, not this one.
dependsOn: The bakery is in the UK, so the Working Time Regulations apply as recorded earlier.
The founder has, or can rebuild, timesheets or clock-in records for the two bakers covering the last eight weeks.
The two bakers really are six-day pre-dawn workers as the brief states, not people whose sixth day is a short shift.

undecidable.question: Are the founder's two bakers night workers under UK rules, and does either currently breach weekly rest, the 48-hour average or the night-work average? This decides whether the fix is a rota tweak, a restructure, or nothing at all.
undecidable.evidenceNeeded: Each baker's actual start and finish times for eight weeks, including any evening-before dough prep; the contract's definition of night time, if any; whether either baker has signed a 48-hour opt-out; and an employment lawyer's reading of whether three or more hours regularly fall inside night time.
undecidable.who: The founder pulls the records, then puts the night-worker question to an employment lawyer (Conor's question, still unanswered in this room).
